new_statements.rule_in_words: Gofa has a Wolaitta/Gamo-type tonal (pitch) accent, not stress: each simple noun, adjective or adverb in citation form carries exactly one High tonal accent whose position is lexically unpredictable — on the final or the penultimate vowel in disyllables (aawá 'father', haré 'donkey', gaammó 'lion' vs boóra 'ox', méhe 'herd', bóllo), antepenult or penult in trisyllables (wónggire 'box', máduntsi 'wound' vs gulbbáta 'knee', wodaáro); in an accented long syllable the H is realised on the second mora; some verb roots are accentless (floating H) and receive their H only from inflectional suffixes; tonal accent also has derivational/grammatical functions (accent shift derives nominals, vocative tonal affix).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described for simple words (only one H per citation form); derived compounds and phrases may carry 'either one or multiple tonal accents' (sec. 5.2.2); phrase-level plateauing spreads H across adjacent syllables/words (sec. 4.3.2.1).
new_statements.exceptions: Verbs behave differently from other word classes (accent depends on affixed inflection; some mono- and polysyllabic roots unaccented, exx. 66, 68); interrogatives add an extra H on the verb-agreement suffix (boundary tone, sec. 4.3.2.2); author notes contour formation, downdrift and downstep are left for future work; low accents deliberately left unmarked.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about citation (absolutive) forms of words, i.e. word-level lexical accent; separate sections treat phrase/sentence-level H-spreading (plateauing) and sentence-type boundary H on the finite verb. Data represent the Sawla dialect (Demba Gofa woreda), p. 11.
new_statements.identity_note: Sellassie Cheru 2015 describes Gofa (gofa1235, ISO gof) on the basis of the Sawla dialect spoken in Demba Gofa woreda (fieldwork also touched Gezze Gofa and Zala); the author treats Gofa as a North Ometo cluster language alongside Wolaitta, Gamo and Dawro and explicitly aligns its tonal-accent system with Wolaitta (Azeb 1996) and Gamo (Hayward 1994). Moreno 1938's 'Ometo' grammatical sketch is likewise Gofa-based.

sources.note: Ch. 4 'Tonology' (pp. 77-93): Gofa is a 'tonal accent language' like Wolaitta, Gamo, Zayse; every simple noun/adjective/adverb in citation form bears exactly one high tonal accent, on the final or the penultimate vowel, assignment lexically unpredictable; H sits on the second mora of an accented long syllable; explicitly 'Gofa is not a stress language'; verbs: some roots accentless (floating H) until inflected; H-spreading (plateauing) across words and an extra boundary H on the finite verb in interrogatives.
